title: API 510 Training in San Francisco Bay Area: Online Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Bay Area vessel inspectors: Richmond and Martinez refineries, renewable fuels reactors and hydrogen plants. Instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in the San Francisco Bay Area: Online Exam Prep for Refinery, Renewable and Hydrogen Plant Vessel Inspectors
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors around the bay

The pressure vessels that keep Bay Area inspectors busy line the shore from Richmond to the Carquinez Strait: hydrocracker reactors and separators, fractionating columns, amine contactors, hydrogen plant drums and, since the refinery conversions, reactors that run on fats and vegetable oils. This page is for the NDT technicians, welding inspectors, former operators and engineers preparing to inspect them under API 510.

There is no Atlantis classroom in the San Francisco Bay Area, so vessel candidates here study online. No Atlantis office or classroom sits in San Francisco, Oakland, Richmond or Martinez: Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and the API 510 course is self-paced, with an instructor who answers questions as they come up. The American Petroleum Institute decides whether you are eligible, administers the API 510 examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. You apply to API yourself, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

What is left of Bay Area refining, and the vessels inside it

EIA's refinery capacity survey, with figures as of January 2026, lists three Bay Area refineries: Chevron's Richmond refinery at 245,271 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation, Martinez Refining Company at Martinez, which PBF Energy bought from Shell, at 156,400, and Valero's Benicia refinery at 145,000. Benicia appears only because it was still running on the survey date. EIA has since reported that Benicia ceased refining and dropped out of its monthly capacity estimates from March 2026, after Valero began idling the process units in February.

The two plants still refining crude differ. EIA lists catalytic cracking, gas oil hydrocracking, catalytic reforming and solvent deasphalting at Richmond but no coking, and coking at Martinez alongside catalytic cracking and hydrocracking. The table maps the area's main unit types to their vessels and to damage mechanisms on the API 510 Body of Knowledge list.

Unit type and where it runsVessels an API 510 inspector meetsMechanisms on the API 510 list to know
Hydrocracking: Richmond, MartinezReactors, hot and cold high-pressure separators, feed/effluent exchanger shellsHigh temperature hydrogen attack, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion, wet H2S damage
Catalytic reforming: Richmond, MartinezReactors, product separators, stabiliser columnsHigh temperature hydrogen attack, hydrochloric acid corrosion
Fluid catalytic cracking: Richmond, MartinezReactor, regenerator, main fractionator, gas plant drumsErosion, sulfidation, wet H2S damage in the gas plant
Amine and sour water systems: every refineryAbsorbers, regenerators, strippers, overhead accumulatorsAmine stress corrosion cracking, wet H2S damage
Hydrogen plants: Richmond, and supplier-run units at Martinez and RodeoSteam drums, shift converters, condensate separatorsBoiler water and steam condensate corrosion, high temperature hydrogen attack
Renewable diesel units: Rodeo, Martinez RenewablesReactors, high-pressure separators, pretreatment vesselsHigh temperature hydrogen attack, hydrochloric acid corrosion; fatty acid attack is not on the list

Hydrogen plants, and the boilers' cousins

Contra Costa Health's list of facilities under the county's Industrial Safety Ordinance includes two Air Products operations, one within the Martinez Refining Company site and one within Martinez Renewable Fuels, and the Air Liquide hydrogen plant at Rodeo. Air Products bought steam methane reformer plants at Martinez from PBF Energy in 2020, and the county describes the Air Products plant at Martinez Renewables as making hydrogen for renewable fuels production. At Richmond, the City Council approved Chevron's Modernization Project in 2014 with a replacement hydrogen plant among its main parts, and the construction contractor describes two steam methane reformers designed to make 230 million standard cubic feet of hydrogen a day.

A reformer plant shows where vessel rules end. Its steam drum, waste heat boiler and deaerator behave like parts of a boiler, and whether each sits in the boiler or the pressure vessel programme depends on how it was designed and stamped and how the owner and jurisdiction classify it. Shift converters and condensate separators are plainer vessel work. Two mechanisms on the API 510 list come straight from these plants: boiler water and steam condensate corrosion, driven by dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide, and high temperature hydrogen attack. Where a supplier runs the hydrogen plant inside a refinery's fence, find out early whose inspection department holds the records.

Reactors that changed feed: the renewable diesel conversions

Two former crude refineries now make renewable fuels. Phillips 66 stopped processing crude at Rodeo in early 2024, according to Argus, and by the middle of that year the complex was producing about 50,000 barrels a day of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel from used cooking oil, fats, greases and vegetable oil, after pretreatment in new units. Marathon's former Martinez refinery is now Martinez Renewables, a joint venture with Neste that Marathon describes as making approximately 730 million gallons a year and reaching full capacity by the end of 2024. Project descriptions in Oil & Gas Journal show how much was meant to stay: at Rodeo two hydrocrackers were to be repurposed, one with replacement reactor vessels, and at Martinez the No. 3 hydrodesulfurizer and the second-stage hydrocracker were among the first units to be modified, while the crude unit, catalytic cracker and coker were scheduled for removal.

A converted reactor carries a long history and an inspection plan written for petroleum service. A 2023 Inspectioneering article on converted units explains that the reaction turns fatty acids and triglycerides into carbon dioxide and water, that fatty acids attack stainless grades without molybdenum, such as the types 321 and 347 common in older hydrotreaters, that chlorides from used cooking oil accelerate the attack, and that carbon dioxide corrosion follows wherever water condenses in the effluent train. High temperature hydrogen attack and creep still apply in the hot reaction section, and brittle fracture and polythionic acid stress corrosion cracking during shutdowns.

Fatty acid corrosion is not on the API 510 list, so the exam will not test it by name. Naphthenic acid corrosion is on the list, though, and it is the closest petroleum relative: another organic acid attack whose severity depends on temperature, velocity and the molybdenum in the alloy. Learn the listed mechanisms for the exam and the renewable ones for the job. API 510 expects the inspection plan to reflect the damage mechanisms of the vessel's current service, so a reactor that changed feed needs its plan rewritten, not rolled forward from the old one.

Who oversees inspection programmes in Contra Costa County

Most Bay Area process plants sit in Contra Costa County, which adds a layer of its own. The county's Industrial Safety Ordinance, Chapter 450-8, adopted in December 1998, applies to refineries and chemical plants in unincorporated areas that file a Risk Management Plan and run at least one Program 3 process; it covers the Air Products, Phillips 66, Air Liquide, Martinez Renewable Fuels and Martinez Refining Company sites. Richmond's matching ordinance, Chapter 6.43, adopted in December 2000, covers the Chevron refinery.

The county's guidance says the ordinance requires facilities to maintain their equipment, including an inspection program, and Contra Costa Health audits each covered facility every three years. Cal/OSHA's refinery standard, Title 8 section 5189.1, applies on top. Neither the county's pages nor the state rule names API 510 or an inspector certification; the owner decides what its inspectors and contractors hold. Benicia, across the strait in Solano County, lies outside the county ordinance.

Worked example: a hemispherical head, static head and the hydrotest

These figures are for practice and describe no real vessel. A vertical drum returning to service after a feed change has a hemispherical bottom head with an inside radius L of 42 in., an allowable stress of 17,100 psi at design temperature given in the problem and E = 1.0. The head's lowest reading is 0.640 in., the corrosion rate is 0.004 in. per year and the next inspection is planned in eight years.

  1. Thickness for the calculation: API 510 takes off twice the corrosion expected before the next inspection, so t = 0.640 − 2 × 0.004 × 8 = 0.576 in.
  2. Head MAWP from UG-32(e), rearranged: P = 2SEt ÷ (L + 0.2t) = 19,699 ÷ 42.115 = about 468 psi at the head.
  3. Static head: the bottom head sits 36 ft below the top of the drum. The Body of Knowledge bases all static head on a specific gravity of 1.0, which gives 0.433 psi per foot, so 36 × 0.433 = 15.6 psi. Measured at the top, this part limits the drum to about 452 psi.
  4. Suppose the shell courses, worked the same way, limit the drum to 440 psi at the top. That is the vessel MAWP, because the lowest part governs.
  5. Test pressure under UG-99: 1.3 × MAWP × LSR, with the stress ratio taken from 20,000 psi at test temperature over 17,100 psi at design temperature, LSR = 1.170. The minimum test pressure is 1.3 × 440 × 1.170 = about 669 psi at the top.

The trap in step five is the gauge. If the drum is tested standing upright and the gauge sits near the bottom head, it reads the top pressure plus the water column, about 685 psi, so a candidate who sets the gauge reading to 669 psi has under-tested the top of the vessel. Exam questions like to hide the gauge location in the wording.

Routes into API 510 from Bay Area jobs

API weighs education against pressure vessel experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year supervising or performing vessel inspection; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of vessels; a high school diploma needs three; and no formal education needs five or more, with at least one year of inspection inside each of the longer routes. The API 510 certification requirements page sets out the detail. Local starting points:

  • Operations technicians. Los Medanos College in Pittsburg runs a process technology programme with certificates and an associate degree, and it lists Chevron, Marathon and ConocoPhillips among the refineries and Dow and Corteva among the chemical companies that hire its graduates. Years operating vessels count towards the longer routes, but you still need a year of inspection before you apply.
  • NDT technicians with thickness and shear wave work on Richmond or Martinez equipment; see NDT training in the San Francisco Bay Area and NDT training in Martinez for the ASNT steps.
  • Welders and welding inspectors from turnaround and repair contractors, whose repair experience counts once a year of inspection sits beside it. The AWS CWI exam prep for the Bay Area page covers the welding inspector route.
  • Graduate engineers in reliability, process or inspection groups at the refineries, renewable plants and hydrogen suppliers.

Studying API 510 from Richmond, Martinez or the South Bay

Bay Area candidates juggle rotating shifts, bridge commutes and turnaround seasons, and self-paced study fits around all three. Pick an exam window clear of your site's next major outage, learn the API 510 code first because the closed-book half leans on it, build the Section VIII calculations until you can work them without notes, then move through RP 571, RP 572, RP 576, RP 577, RP 578, Section V, Section IX and PCC-2, in the editions on your window's effectivity sheet.

If a renewable unit's plan cites a mechanism you cannot find in RP 571, or a hydrogen plant drum is treated differently from the way you expected, send it to the instructor, who answers from the code text. Prometric's test centre list covers the Bay Area; book early in the window, at a centre you can reach without a morning bridge crossing.

Preparation options in the Bay Area, compared

  • College programmes. Los Medanos College trains plant operators, and welding programmes build the background RP 577 and Section IX assume; neither is API exam preparation.
  • Employer programmes. Larger owner-users sometimes pair candidates with a certified inspector. Ask your supervisor before paying yourself.
  • Intensive seminars before each window, which suit candidates who already know the codes and can leave site for consecutive days. Ask who answers questions afterwards.
  • Self-paced online study with instructor Q&A, the Atlantis format, which suits shift workers and anyone who needs to repeat the calculations.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Bay Area site

Refinery inspection groups, the renewable fuels plants, the hydrogen suppliers and the contractors that staff Bay Area turnarounds can enrol several candidates at once, and each works at their own pace. Eligibility is personal, so check each candidate's record against API's rules first. We quote fees on request, whether for a single vessel inspector or a whole group. Piping and tank candidates can join the same enquiry; the API 510 training overview explains the course.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 class I can attend in person in the Bay Area?
faq.a: Not with Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in the San Francisco Bay Area, and the API 510 course is self-paced online study with an instructor who answers your questions. Whichever way you prepare, API holds the examination in person at a Prometric test centre once it has accepted your application.

faq.q: Does the Contra Costa Industrial Safety Ordinance require API 510 inspectors?
faq.a: The county's ordinance pages describe a requirement to maintain equipment with an inspection program, and Contra Costa Health audits covered facilities every three years, but they do not name API 510 or any inspector certification. Refiners commonly run their vessel programmes to API 510, and each owner decides which certification it expects from its own inspectors and from contractors.

faq.q: Do the renewable diesel plants at Rodeo and Martinez still need API 510 inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. Both plants run hydroprocessing reactors, high-pressure separators, exchangers and pretreatment vessels, much of it carried over from their refinery days. The feed has changed, which brings fatty acid corrosion, chlorides from used cooking oil and carbon dioxide corrosion into the inspection plan, but the vessels still need inspecting, rerating and repairing under the same code.

faq.q: Are hydrogen plant steam drums inspected under API 510?
faq.a: It depends on how the drum was built and how the owner and jurisdiction classify it. Steam drums and waste heat boilers in steam methane reformer plants often sit under boiler rules, while shift converters, separators and adsorber vessels are usually pressure vessel programme work. Boiler water and steam condensate corrosion is on the API 510 Body of Knowledge list, so the exam expects you to know the mechanism either way.

faq.q: Does operating experience from a refinery or chemical plant job count towards API 510?
faq.a: Operating pressure vessels counts as experience for the two-, three- and five-year routes, which accept design, construction, repair, operation or inspection, but each of those routes also needs at least one year supervising or performing vessel inspection. A process technician who moves into an inspection group can usually build that year on site. API verifies the experience you document in the application.

faq.q: Is fatty acid corrosion on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: No. The Body of Knowledge lists a fixed set of RP 571 mechanisms, among them naphthenic acid corrosion, high temperature hydrogen attack, chloride stress corrosion cracking and wet H2S damage, and fatty acid attack is not one of them. If you work at Rodeo or Martinez Renewables, learn it for the job, and learn naphthenic acid corrosion for the exam: the two behave in similar ways.

faq.q: What happens to vessel inspection at Benicia now that refining has stopped?
faq.a: EIA reports that Benicia ceased refining and left its monthly capacity estimates from March 2026. Idle vessels still need isolation, preservation and records, and the site's future is Valero's decision. Steady API 510 work in the region sits at Richmond, Martinez, the renewable fuels and hydrogen plants and their contractors.

faq.q: Where do Bay Area candidates sit the API 510 exam?
faq.a: At a Prometric test centre, in person, after API approves your application. Pick a centre from Prometric's Bay Area listings when you schedule. The day runs about 7.5 hours, with a closed-book part, a lunch break and an open-book part where the code PDFs are on screen. You may not bring books or notes. The API exam schedule page lists the windows and their deadlines.
